title: How To Handle A Student Who Rejects Your Kindness
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In a more reflective, personal essay, Linsin writes to teachers whose sustained kindness toward a particular student is repeatedly met with indifference or cruelty, acknowledging the very real hurt and simmering anger this provokes. He reframes the student's rejection as likely self-protective, suggesting they may have been burned so often that accepting a teacher's care feels too risky given the possibility of eventual disappointment. His counsel is not a specific technique but a posture: breathe, suppress the urge toward retaliation, remember one's own struggles, and keep offering steady kindness regardless of whether or when it is accepted. He frames unwavering patience and consistency, without expectation of reciprocity, as the essential and defining work of teaching.
points: Names the genuine hurt and anger teachers feel when sustained kindness toward a student is met with indifference or cruelty.
Reframes a student's rejection of kindness as likely self-protective rather than personal, given a history of being let down.
Counsels teachers to consciously suppress retaliatory urges and recall their own past struggles and pain.
Frames continued, unwavering kindness—offered without expectation of reciprocity—as the essential work of teaching.
Suggests acceptance may come on any timeline, from a week to the very last day of school, and that persistence matters regardless.
quotes: They meet your smile, your generosity, and your kindness with indifference—and even cruelty.
You daydream about putting them in their place. You lay awake rehearsing a lecture they won’t soon forget.
Maybe they’ve been burned so many times and so deeply that if they allow themselves to like you—or worse, look up to you—and you let them down, the blow would be too great.
Maybe they’ve erected a hard shell over shattered trust and the possibility of disappointment and betrayal.
You give your patience and your understanding. You give your steadiness and your consistency. You give your unrelenting, unbending, undefeatable kindness.
Maybe this will be the day they accept you and let you in. Maybe it will be in a week or a month or on the last day of school.
